justice: Spatial resources are unevenly distributed because most usable width is given to mixed vehicle movement and parking, while no formal sidewalk is visible on either side.
Fairness is weakened by parked vans, cars, and a blue truck occupying the edge space that pedestrians would otherwise use along the building frontage.
Accessibility is poor because the road surface is unpaved and uneven, with loose dirt and rough edges that would be difficult for many users to traverse.
The right side has a fence and narrow dirt edge beside vegetation, but this margin does not function as an accessible pedestrian facility.
No curb ramps, tactile paving, marked crossings, or designated universal-access elements are visible in the scene.
safety: Safety is reduced by the lack of a separated pedestrian path, forcing walkers to share the same narrow carriageway with vans, cars, and small trucks.
The dusty, uneven road surface can increase skidding and tripping risk for all road users, especially where the edge crumbles near the fence line.
Dense overhead utility wires and crowded poles suggest poor streetscape maintenance, which can contribute to a general sense of infrastructure hazard.
There are no visible lane markings, speed-calming devices, or crossings to organize movement and reduce conflicts.
Parked vehicles along the left side narrow sightlines and can create sudden conflicts when vehicles enter or leave parking spaces.
livability: Livability is limited because the street appears dominated by service access and parking rather than people-oriented public space.
Closed shutters along the ground floor reduce visible active frontage and diminish street vitality at the time of capture.
The fenced green edge and trees on the right provide some environmental relief and slight buffering from the adjacent open area.
Basic commercial frontage does exist on the left, which may support local daily needs even though the pedestrian environment is weak.
The overall dusty condition, narrow road, and lack of seating or social space make the street less suitable for lingering and everyday social use.
sustainability: Street trees and planted shrubs on the right contribute some greenery and limited ecological value compared with a fully hardscaped corridor.
However, the road design does not visibly support sustainable transport because there is no dedicated sidewalk, bike lane, or public-transit stop in view.
The unpaved dusty surface may increase particulate pollution and indicates low-quality long-term infrastructure provision.
The linear green strip beside the fence offers minor stormwater infiltration potential, though no formal drainage or rain-garden features are visible.
Frequent vehicle parking and mixed motor traffic suggest continued dependence on private and service vehicles.
aesthetics: Aesthetic quality is weakened by extensive tangled overhead wires that dominate the skyline and create visual clutter.
The unfinished or weathered building facades and multiple closed metal shutters give the corridor a worn appearance.
The dusty road surface and rough edges reduce visual neatness and perceived maintenance quality.
Trees and shrubs along the right side add some softness and natural color, partially offsetting the harsh built environment.
The distant high-rise skyline provides some visual depth, but the immediate foreground remains visually disorderly.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: trees on the right provide partial shade, but most of the road and left frontage are exposed to direct sun.
Physical comfort is poor because the travel surface is rough, dusty, and uneven, with no paved pedestrian zone or seating visible.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the need to share a narrow roadway with moving and parked vehicles in an unorganized traffic environment.
The fence and vegetation on the right create a slight buffer from the adjacent open space, which modestly improves environmental comfort.
Visual clutter from utility cables and the generally neglected streetscape can lower perceived ease and calm for everyday users.
walkability: Walkability is very low because there is no continuous sidewalk visible on either side of the street.
Pedestrians would need to walk within the same corridor used by moving vehicles and roadside parking, increasing conflict and reducing comfort.
The dirt and uneven edge conditions do not support smooth, stable walking routes for daily travel.
No marked crossings, curb extensions, wayfinding, or pedestrian-priority treatments are visible.
Some shade from the right-side trees helps slightly, but it does not compensate for the lack of basic pedestrian infrastructure.
bikeability: Bikeability is poor because there is no bike lane, shoulder, or protected cycling space anywhere in the corridor.
Cyclists would have to mix directly with vans, trucks, and cars on a narrow road with no lane definition.
The dusty and uneven road surface would reduce riding stability and comfort, especially near the edge conditions.
Parked vehicles on the left create dooring and pull-out conflict risks for people cycling through the street.
No bicycle parking, markings, signage, or intersection treatments are visible to support safe or convenient cycling.
